articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Actions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.

This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting illicit financial networks that support criminal and terrorist organizations globally. The specific details of the designated parties and their activities were not immediately released but are expected to be detailed in forthcoming OFAC guidance.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update, Targeting Sanctions Evasion Networks
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026, as part of its ongoing efforts to counter Iranian sanctions evasion. This action specifically targeted 13 individuals and companies linked to a network providing fraudulent vessel flags and maritime certifications to Iran's 'shadow fleet'.

The designated network, reportedly led by Suniel Kumar Sharma and Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, is accused of facilitating the transport of Iranian petroleum, including for Iran's military and its proxies. OFAC highlighted that vessels using false flags lack valid protection and indemnity insurance, posing significant risks to maritime stakeholders.

Concurrently with these designations, OFAC also issued an alert warning maritime stakeholders about the risks associated with Iran's 'shadow fleet' and its reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Eight Canadian Money Services Businesses for Iran-Related Activities
body: On November 6, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated eight Canada-based money services businesses for allegedly operating in the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy. These businesses are accused of exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets.

Many of the designated entities reportedly dealt with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). This action was coordinated with FinCEN, Canada's financial intelligence unit, and the Drug Enforcement Administration.

OFAC stated that several of these businesses facilitated transactions for Ryan Wedding, a sanctioned Canadian and former Olympic snowboarder, who allegedly trafficked narcotics and used money services businesses to move drug proceeds abroad as digital assets.

articles.headline: OFAC Expands Cuba Sanctions to Key Economic Sectors and Targets Cyber-related Criminal Organizations
body: On November 5, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a determination under Executive Order 14404, authorizing sanctions against foreign persons operating in Cuba's electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors.

This action was taken in conjunction with the State Department's designation of eight entities and two individuals, and the identification of five vessels, for supporting Cuba's oil shipping networks, state-owned entities, and military supply chains.

Additionally, OFAC sanctioned four individuals and 41 entities supporting the Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization, targeting corporate and financial networks involved in cyber scams, illicit proceeds laundering, and sanctions evasion. A Malaysian individual accused of managing an Africa-based scam network targeting U.S. victims was also designated.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations and Amends Venezuela-Related General License
body: On November 4, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings. This action is part of Operation Economic Outcast, targeting networks involved in operating fraudulent ship registries that facilitate sanctions evasion by Iran's 'shadow fleet'.

OFAC also published an Iran-related alert, warning about the substantial risk of designation or penalties for providing services to vessels using false flags to evade U.S. sanctions on Iran. The alert highlighted the use of fraudulent registries and 'flag hopping' by the Iranian shadow fleet.

In a separate action, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, authorizing certain transactions, financing, and other dealings involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5% bond on or after December 18, 2026. This license replaces General License 5Z, and OFAC also amended FAQ 595 to reflect the updated authorization.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: U.S. Wholesale Inflation Rises to Highest Annual Rate in Nearly Four Years
body: U.S. wholesale inflation, as measured by the Producer Price Index (PPI), accelerated in October to its highest annual rate in nearly four years.

The PPI rose 0.3% from the previous month and 6.5% for the 12 months ending in October, marking the highest annual rate since November 2022. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, core PPI increased 0.3% monthly and 5% annually, matching a rate last seen in January 2023.

High energy prices, particularly for gas and diesel, driven by the ongoing Iran war, have been a significant factor contributing to the rise in wholesale inflation, which is expected to ripple through supply chains and potentially lead to further consumer price increases.

Energy prices are expected to have the highest annual rate in October at 20.8%, followed by services at 3.3%, food, alcohol & tobacco at 1.6%, and non-energy industrial goods at 1.2%.
This continued acceleration in inflation, particularly driven by energy costs, puts pressure on the European Central Bank (ECB) as it navigates its monetary policy decisions.

body: Senior Iranian officials reportedly believe the United States is planning either further military strikes or an intensified economic stranglehold that could provoke retaliatory action from Tehran.

Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's chief negotiator, stated that the Americans had proposed a two-week timeframe for President Donald Trump to decide on military action. Mohammadi expressed doubt about Trump's claims that the military option was off the table, suggesting Washington was preparing for a limited strike.

Mohammadi also indicated that Iran had rejected a request from U.S. Vice President JD Vance for a direct meeting with Iranian negotiators, and that Iran's latest proposals on reopening the Strait of Hormuz were deemed 'unsatisfactory and completely deceptive' by the U.S.

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' Until January 10, 2027
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced on November 9, 2026, an extension of the suspension of its 'Affiliates Rule' until January 10, 2027.

The 'Affiliates Rule,' originally published in September 2025, expands export control restrictions under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to foreign entities that are 50% owned or controlled by parties on certain restricted lists, even if those entities are not explicitly named.

This extension provides businesses with additional time to ensure their compliance systems are updated to meet the new requirements, which are designed to harmonize BIS ownership and control restrictions with similar rules enforced by OFAC's '50% Rule'.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
This deregulatory action shifts control of these items from the State Department's U.S. Munitions List to the EAR, aligning their export controls with those already applied to firearms.
The change aims to streamline the export process for these items, potentially reducing administrative burdens for manufacturers and exporters.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
